title: David and Jonathan (1 Samuel 18–20)
hookLine: a prince loves David as his own soul and warns him with arrows

cards: On paper, these two should be rivals. One is Jonathan, King Saul's son and heir, a brave soldier in his own right. The other is David, who just killed Goliath.
After the battle the women of Israel come out dancing with a song: Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. Saul hears it and something sours in him.
From that day, the text says, he keeps a jealous eye on David. Jonathan is the one who stands to lose a kingdom. Instead, something else happens.

teach.b: It begins in one sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Knit. The Hebrew verb means tied or bound together, the word for a knot.
The two make a covenant, a solemn promise before God.

teach.h: A PRINCE GIVES AWAY HIS ROBE.
teach.b: And Jonathan seals it with a gesture: he takes off his own robe and gives it to David, then his armor, his sword, his bow and his belt. The heir to the throne hands the shepherd the clothes of a prince.
Then Saul's jealousy turns murderous. He throws a spear at David and orders his servants to kill him.

Jonathan is caught between his father and his friend. He doesn't pretend the danger isn't real, and he abandons neither of them. He speaks up for David to his father's face, and his father hurls a spear at him too.
Then comes the plan with the arrows. David hides in a field. Jonathan goes out to shoot with a boy.
If he calls, the arrows are on this side of you, David is safe. If he calls, the arrows are beyond you, David must run.
Jonathan shoots, and calls out: the arrow is beyond thee.

teach.h: HE LOVED HIM AS HIS OWN SOUL.
teach.b: The boy runs off with the arrows, knowing nothing. The two friends meet, kiss and weep, David most of all. They part with a promise: the Lord be between me and thee for ever.
In the twelfth century, the English abbot Aelred of Rievaulx held these two up in his book on spiritual friendship: loyal when it costs a crown, honest when it's dangerous, and bound before God.

how: Catholics hear part of the David and Jonathan story at weekday Mass early in Ordinary Time, in one year of the two-year cycle (1 Samuel 18–19).

o: the soul, the whole living self
the heart, where a person decides
the breath God blew into Adam

games.q: the prince and the shepherd — tap the pairs.
p: how their two souls were joined
grew jealous of David's ten thousands

s: Jonathan saw David as a rival for the throne
he loved him as his own soul, and gave him his robe and weapons.
Jonathan used arrows to signal that David must flee
"the arrow is beyond thee" meant David had to go.
the boy who fetched the arrows knew the secret
the text says he knew nothing; only Jonathan and David knew.

games.q: you're Jonathan, the crown prince. your father wants your best friend dead, and your friend is the one people say will be king. what do you do?
o: side with your father; it's your throne.
stay quiet and let things play out.
speak up for David, and warn him to escape.
games.why: Jonathan defends David to Saul's face, then warns him with the arrows. loyalty that costs him a crown, sealed with a covenant before the Lord.

practice: Bring to mind a friend who stood by you when it cost them something, who spoke up for you in a room you weren't in, or stayed when leaving was easier.
Picture their face, remember one specific thing they did, and let yourself feel how much it mattered. If you pray, thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: nefesh. Hebrew for soul, the whole living self: Jonathan loved David as his own nefesh, bound by a covenant that cost him a crown. Today's word.
